strengths: Well-motivated and novel idea: using traversal orders of uniform spanning trees over the image lattice provides a principled middle ground between fixed raster-scan order (locality/center-bias prior but no flexibility) and random permutation (flexibility but loss of locality/prior structure).

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper connects the method to graph theory (uniform spanning trees, Wilson's algorithm for efficient sampling, BFS vs. DFS tie-breaking analysis), and provides an explicit rejection-sampling algorithm (Algorithm 1) with a proof-sketch style justification (depth condition, Eq. 3) for postfix completion during editing.

Empirical motivation is supported by data: prediction-entropy analyses (Fig. 3, 4, and Appendix Fig. A) under random permutation training show token difficulty correlates with center bias/locality, substantiating the design choice to prioritize spanning-tree structured orders.

Strong quantitative results across four model scales (STAR-B/L/XL/XXL) on ImageNet-1k 256x256 class-conditional generation, matching or outperforming comparable-size SOTA discrete AR baselines (RAR, VAR, LlamaGen, RandAR) with minimal architectural change (only additive positional embeddings for the next-token position).

Convincing inpainting/postfix-completion evaluation across a range of masking ratios (0.1-0.9), with both quantitative (FID/IS/Precision/Recall) and qualitative comparisons showing STAR clearly outperforms the raster-scan RAR baseline for editing, which is a task conventional unidirectional AR models handle poorly.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 2 on order randomization strategy across training/inference stages, Table 3 on BFS vs. DFS and root-selection strategies for rejection-sampling efficiency) that isolate the contribution of the spanning-tree structure versus pure randomization/order annealing.

Reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, masking strategy pseudocode, and extended qualitative samples are provided in the supplementary material; changes to the base Decoder-only Causal AR Transformer are minimal and clearly described.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single dataset/resolution (ImageNet-1k, 256x256, class-conditional generation); there is no demonstration on text-to-image, higher-resolution, or more diverse/naturalistic editing benchmarks, which limits evidence of broader impact and generalizability of the claimed prior-knowledge benefits.

The inpainting comparison is restricted essentially to RAR; other relevant bidirectional or randomized-order baselines shown in Table 1 (e.g., MAR, RandAR, VAR, or mask-based generative models like MaskGIT) are not evaluated on the editing task, so the claimed superiority for image editing is only demonstrated against one competitor.

No analysis of the computational/inference-time overhead introduced by the rejection-sampling procedure for postfix completion (Algorithm 1), despite Table 3 showing the number of trials needed can be substantial at certain masking ratios (e.g., ~60 trials at 0.1 ratio with random root); this could matter for practical deployment.

The gains in class-conditional generation quality over comparable-size raster-scan/randomized AR baselines (e.g., STAR-XXL vs RAR-XXL) are relatively incremental rather than dramatic, so the primary practical contribution is arguably the editing capability rather than raw generation quality.

Limited discussion of failure cases, limitations, or scenarios where the spanning-tree order might underperform (e.g., very large masks, non-connected/partial masks, or editing operations beyond inpainting such as outpainting or semantic edits), and no societal-impact discussion.

Some technical figures (e.g., Fig. 3/4 and Appendix Fig. A) are dense and would benefit from clearer exposition of their practical implications for readers less familiar with spanning-tree/entropy analysis.

strengths: The core idea—using traversal orders of uniform spanning trees (BFS from a random corner) as a structured randomization strategy for AR sequence order—is novel and well-motivated. It elegantly interpolates between fixed raster-scan order (which preserves locality/center-bias priors but is unidirectional) and fully random permutation (which is flexible but degrades performance), addressing a genuine limitation identified in prior work (RAR, RandAR).

The motivating analysis (Figures 3 and 4, and Appendix C) empirically supports the design choice by showing that prediction entropy correlates with spatial locality and center-bias, giving a principled basis for preferring spanning-tree orders over unconstrained random permutations.

The postfix-completion mechanism via rejection sampling of spanning trees conditioned on a connected unmasked region (Algorithm 1) is a thoughtful, theoretically grounded contribution that directly enables image inpainting/editing with an AR model, a capability that conventional raster-scan or naively-trained random-permutation AR models lack.

Experimental results are quite comprehensive: class-conditional generation on ImageNet at multiple model scales (STAR-B/L/XL/XXL) shows STAR is competitive with or better than SOTA (RAR, VAR, LlamaGen, RandAR) at comparable parameter counts, and the inpainting comparison against RAR across varying mask ratios (with qualitative examples) is convincing that STAR provides substantially better bidirectional/postfix completion capability.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 2 on order randomization strategy, Table 3 on BFS vs DFS and root-selection strategy for rejection sampling efficiency) support the specific design decisions (BFS traversal, farthest-root heuristic) with quantitative justification.

The method requires minimal architectural changes to a standard decoder-only causal AR Transformer (only additional positional embeddings for the next-token position), which is an appealing practical advantage for adoption and integration with existing AR pipelines, including potentially early-fusion multimodal models.

The paper is generally clearly written, with a good structure connecting motivation (Section 3.1/3.2), method (3.2/3.3), and empirical validation, and includes reasonable implementation/reproducibility details (Appendix A) and additional qualitative samples (Appendix D).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification connecting the uniform spanning tree to 'prior knowledge such as center bias and locality' is somewhat informal/conjectural (framed as a 'plausible conjecture' in Section 3.2); while empirical entropy analysis is provided as indirect support, there is no rigorous derivation showing why spanning-tree traversal orders are the 'right' structured subset of random permutations as opposed to other structured alternatives.

The evaluation is limited to a single dataset/resolution (ImageNet-1k, 256×256) and a single tokenizer (MaskGIT-VQGAN); it remains unclear how well the approach scales to higher resolutions, other datasets (e.g., text-to-image generation), or continuous tokenizers, which limits the evidence for broader impact claims made in the introduction (e.g., early-fusion multimodal models).

The image editing/inpainting evaluation is restricted to random connected-mask inpainting; more realistic or diverse editing tasks (e.g., outpainting, free-form irregular masks, text-guided edits) are not explored, so the claimed 'image editing' capability is only partially validated.

The rejection-sampling procedure for postfix completion (Table 3) shows non-trivial average trial counts that grow rapidly at low masking ratios (e.g., ~60 trials at ratio 0.1 for random-root BFS), and while the farthest-root heuristic mitigates this, computational overhead/inference-time cost of this sampling procedure relative to baselines is not clearly quantified or discussed (e.g., wall-clock time overhead vs. RAR).

Comparison partners for the inpainting task are limited to RAR only; other bidirectional or diffusion-based baselines with established inpainting capabilities (e.g., MaskGIT, diffusion models) are not included, making it harder to contextualize how competitive STAR's editing performance is against the broader landscape of models designed for inpainting.

The paper does not provide confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or variance information for the reported FID/IS/Precision/Recall numbers, common in generative modeling papers, which slightly limits the strength of the quantitative comparisons, particularly for the ablation tables which have fairly small numerical gaps between configurations.

strengths: Well-motivated and elegant idea: restricting the search space from the full N! permutations to the exp(N) space of uniform spanning trees on a lattice, structurally injecting prior knowledge (center bias, locality) into permutation AR modeling. The connection to well-known results on spanning tree counting/sampling (Wilson's algorithm) is nicely leveraged.

Strong empirical results: STAR matches or outperforms raster-scan AR (LlamaGen, RAR) and random-permutation AR (RandAR) baselines on ImageNet-1k class-conditional generation (FID/IS/P/R) while adding only minimal architectural overhead (only next-token position conditioning), and clearly outperforms other methods on native image inpainting without requiring token dropping/teacher forcing hacks used for DiT or RAR.

Thorough ablations and analysis: entropy analysis (Fig. 3, 8) linking spanning-tree traversal order to conditional model entropy patterns similar to raster-scan; center-bias quartile analysis; DFS vs BFS rejection-sampling trial/failure-rate comparison (Table 4) justifying design choices; sequence-order annealing ablation (Table 3); overhead quantification (<0.0004% of inference time).

The paper is generally clearly written, with a good high-level figure (Fig. 2) and an algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) of the rejection sampling procedure for postfix completion, aiding reproducibility. Hyperparameters and compute budgets (A100 GPU-days) are reported in the appendix.

The representation-learning experiment (Section 5, Fig. 9) is a nice additional piece of evidence that spanning-tree order also helps mitigate overfitting/improve linear-probe accuracy relative to raster-scan, suggesting the idea has value beyond generation quality alone.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-1k 256x256 class-conditional generation; no results on text-to-image or higher-resolution generation are provided, despite the paper's motivation citing multimodal/early-fusion models. This limits evidence for broader impact/generality of the claimed contribution.

The inpainting comparison (Table 2, Fig. 6-7) uses only masking ratios and random connected masks; there is no evaluation on realistic, application-driven editing tasks (e.g., object removal/insertion with semantically meaningful masks, editing benchmarks), so it's unclear how STAR performs in more practical image-editing use cases beyond synthetic random-mask inpainting.

The core method assumes the mask does not disconnect the graph and does not cover all lattice corners (Eq. 5-related constraint); violations require a multi-turn decomposition discussed only briefly in the appendix (Fig. A) without quantitative evaluation, leaving open how much this limitation affects real editing workflows.

Rejection sampling for spanning-tree construction, while shown to be cheap on average, could have heavier tails or failure modes for adversarial/complex mask shapes; Table 4 measures trials/failures only for random masks with ratios up to 0.9, not for structured or disconnected masks that are common in real editing (e.g., non-convex regions, multiple disjoint small holes).

Some choices (e.g., regular taxicab lattice as the sole graph structure, corner root selection, learnable positional embeddings vs. RoPE) are not deeply justified with alternative-design ablations beyond the DFS/BFS and root-selection comparisons; e.g., no ablation comparing to other structured sub-permutation spaces (e.g., Hilbert curve family, hierarchical/quad-tree orders) which would better substantiate that spanning trees are the best middle ground rather than just a reasonable one.

Comparisons in Table 1/2 involve models trained under possibly different compute/data budgets across baselines (parameter counts differ), and while FID gains are consistent, the improvements over RAR/RandAR at comparable model sizes are sometimes modest (e.g., STAR-XL FID 1.65 vs. RAR-XL FID 1.50 in Table 1), which is not explicitly acknowledged as a case where STAR underperforms in generation-only metrics despite superior inpainting.

strengths: The core idea of constraining the sequence-order sample space of permutation AR modeling to BFS traversals of uniform spanning trees is well-motivated: it structurally encodes prior knowledge about images (center bias, locality) that random permutation lacks, while retaining enough diversity to support flexible inpainting/editing order, unlike fixed raster-scan.

The method requires only minimal architectural changes to the standard decoder-only Transformer (position conditioning only), making it easy to adopt and consistent with the goal of preserving compatibility with early-fusion multimodal LLM-style architectures.

The rejection-sampling algorithm for selecting a spanning tree/traversal that guarantees the given partial (masked) observation forms a valid prefix is a nontrivial and useful technical contribution, and the paper carefully proves/justifies why BFS (over DFS) is the right traversal choice via the depth-monotonicity condition (Eq. 5) and empirically shows BFS needs far fewer rejection trials (Table 4).

Empirical results are reasonably comprehensive: class-conditional generation on ImageNet-1k at multiple model scales (B/L/XL/XXL) achieves FID/IS/Precision/Recall competitive with or exceeding recent raster-scan and randomized-order AR baselines (LlamaGen, RAR, RandAR) without added training complexity such as sequence-order annealing (Table 1).

Image inpainting comparisons against DiT, RAR, and RandAR (Table 2, Fig. 6, Fig. 7) show STAR retains inpainting quality much closer to its generation quality than diffusion or raster-scan AR baselines, supporting the paper's central claim of preserving native postfix completion.

The ablation studies are thoughtful and go beyond simple accuracy numbers: conditional model entropy analysis (Fig. 3, Fig. 8b) and center-bias quartile analysis (Fig. 8a) directly probe the mechanism behind why spanning-tree order helps, rather than just reporting end metrics.

A representation-learning probe (Fig. 9) is included as an additional signal that spanning-tree ordering may have benefits beyond generation/inpainting FID, which is a nice touch of due diligence beyond the main claims.

The paper reports overhead analysis (rejection sampling trial counts, wall-clock overhead <0.0004%), suggesting the practical cost of the added complexity is low, which supports reproducibility and adoption.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee for postfix completion (Algorithm 1, Eq. 5) explicitly assumes the mask does not touch all corners and does not disconnect the non-masked region into separate components; the paper acknowledges (Appendix A) this is a real limitation requiring a multi-turn decomposition workaround that is not implemented or empirically evaluated, only illustrated with a single qualitative example (Fig. A), leaving the general editing use case less rigorously validated.

The experimental evaluation of inpainting is restricted to synthetic random connected masks at controlled masking ratios, rather than realistic, structured editing masks (e.g., object removal/insertion, arbitrary user-drawn masks) that would better demonstrate the claimed image-editing motivation.

Model scale in the main comparisons tops out at STAR-XXL (1.5B) at 256x256 resolution only; there is no evaluation at higher resolutions or of text-to-image / multimodal generation, which is stated as a motivating use case (early-fusion multimodal models) but never empirically tested.

The paper does not report wall-clock/sampling speed comparisons against baselines (only relative overhead of the tree sampling step itself), so it's unclear how the method compares in practical inference latency to raster-scan AR or diffusion baselines beyond FID/IS.

Some choices (e.g., learnable positional embeddings rather than RoPE or other position encodings for next-token position conditioning) are explicitly left untested, which is stated as future work but limits the completeness of the architectural ablations.

The tie-breaking rule for BFS and alternative traversal/rejection strategies are noted as "not widely explored," indicating the specific algorithmic choices, while empirically justified to some degree, are not exhaustively ablated against other plausible alternatives.
